title: 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho'
summary: The road in the parable drops about a kilometre in vertical height over some 27 km of bare limestone gorge, and Luke's 'down' and 'up' match it.
body: Jericho sits at roughly 250 m below sea level, the lowest city on earth. Jerusalem stands at about 750 m above it. The Roman-period road between them ran some 27 km through the Judean wilderness, climbing about 1,000 m — an average gradient near 4%, with much steeper stretches. Luke's 'going down' and 'going up' (Luke 10:30; 19:28) match the ground.

The route threads the head of the Wadi Qelt, a narrow limestone gorge with blind bends and high sides. Joshua 18:17 names the ascent of Adummim, the red ascent. Josephus describes the descent to Jericho as rugged and desolate.

The Babylonian Talmud records that when each of the twenty-four priestly watches went up for its week of temple service, 'half the priestly watch would ascend from all over Eretz Yisrael to Jerusalem, and half the priestly watch would ascend from Jericho' (Taanit 27a). The parable's first two travellers are a priest and a Levite.
The elevations are modern survey figures and the road length depends on which line you trace; both are given here as approximations.

title: Why the Sea of Galilee turns violent so fast
summary: A lake 210 m below sea level, ringed by highlands 700 to 2,800 m above it. Meteorologists describe strong winds and a storm on the lake almost every summer afternoon, and rarer easterly storms, mostly at night between November and May, that raise hazardous waves.
body: The lake is small: about 21 km long, 13 km wide, 43 m deep at most. Its surface sits roughly 210 m below sea level, in a rift valley. To the east the Golan plateau rises to more than 700 m within a few kilometres of the shore; to the north-east Mount Hermon reaches 2,814 m.

P. Alpert and his colleagues (1982) modelled the air flowing from the Mediterranean past the lake in summer, to explain what they call two striking features of its weather: 'the almost daily development of strong winds and an associated storm on the lake in the afternoon', and a drop in wind speed of nearly half from the western shore to the eastern, over only 10 km. Shubham Pachpor and his colleagues (2026) studied the easterly storms: 24 between 2000 and 2024 with winds of at least 10 m/s for two hours or more, most of them at night, lasting under twelve hours, between November and May, and generating 'hazardous waves' on the lake.
The Gospels tell of more than one storm on the lake. In Mark 4:39 what stops is both the wind and the waves.
The physical measurements are survey data. Neither study describes a storm of the Gospels' time.

title: Gehenna is a valley, and where the rubbish-dump story begins
summary: The word behind 'hell' in the Gospels is Ge-Hinnom, a real ravine on the south-west side of Jerusalem. The explanation that it was a perpetually burning garbage dump goes back, Lloyd Bailey found, to a rabbi writing about AD 1200, with no earlier evidence for it.
body: Gehenna transliterates the Aramaic Ge-Hinnam, from Hebrew Ge ben-Hinnom, 'the valley of the son of Hinnom'. It is a specific place: the ravine curving round the south and west of the Old City, meeting the Kidron below the City of David. In Joshua 15:8 and 18:16 it is simply a boundary marker.

What made the name terrible is what happened there. 2 Kings 23:10 says Josiah defiled Topheth 'which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, so that no one could make his son or his daughter pass through the fire to Molech'; 2 Chronicles 28:3 and 33:6 name Ahaz and Manasseh as kings who did. Jeremiah 7:31-32 and 19:6 pronounce that the place will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter and used as a burial ground until there is no room left. By the intertestamental period (1 Enoch 27, 90) the valley's name had become the name of the place of final judgement, and that is how the Gospels use it.

Lloyd Bailey (1986) looked for the dump in the ancient sources and found no reference in the Hebrew Bible, the Apocrypha, Josephus, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Mishnah or the Talmud to Jerusalem's refuse being burned in the Hinnom valley, and no archaeological deposit of the kind identified there. The earliest statement of it he found is in Rabbi David Kimhi's commentary on Psalm 27, written around AD 1200, more than a millennium after the Gospels.

title: You always go up to Jerusalem
summary: Scripture speaks of going up to Jerusalem and down from it regardless of the compass direction — from Galilee in the north, from Jericho in the east, from Egypt in the south. The city stands on a ridge.
body: Jerusalem sits on the central hill country at roughly 750 m above sea level, with ground falling away on three sides: to the Jordan rift in the east, the Shephelah and coastal plain in the west, and the desert in the south. Every approach is a climb. So Galileans travelling south 'go up' (Luke 2:42), Paul returning from Antioch in the north 'goes up' (Acts 15:2), and the good Samaritan's traveller heading east and downhill 'goes down' (Luke 10:30).

The Hebrew verb alah, 'go up', became the technical term for pilgrimage; the three pilgrim feasts are the regalim, and the noun aliyah, 'a going up', is still the ordinary Hebrew word for immigrating to the land and for being called up to read the Torah.

Psalms 120-134 carry the heading shir hammaalot, 'a song of ascents'. The Mishnah sets the Levites with their instruments on the fifteen steps between the temple's courts, 'corresponding to the fifteen Songs of the Ascents' (Sukkah 5:4). The heading has also been read as pilgrims' songs on the way up, or as a poetic device in which each verse steps up from the last.

title: Joel's locusts, photographed in 1915
summary: In spring 1915 a locust plague stripped Palestine. Photographers of Jerusalem's American Colony recorded it stage by stage: the swarms, the crawling young, and the trees left bare.
body: Joel names four kinds of locust (1:4, 2:25). They have been read as four species and as stages of one insect's growth. In a plague, adults lay eggs, and the young that hatch, wingless and crawling, eat what the swarm left before they can fly; the 1915 photographers called the crawling stage 'most destructive'.

The American Colony photographers titled their series 'The terrible plague of locusts in Palestine, March–June 1915'. It shows masses of locusts on an olive tree, locusts devouring palm leaves, storks in pursuit of the swarm, and the Garden of Gethsemane before and after.

Joel 1:7 says the swarm 'has stripped off the bark … the branches have turned white', and 2:7-9 that the locusts 'scale the walls', 'run along the wall' and 'climb into houses, entering through windows like thieves'. The photographs show trees stripped bare. Joel 2:10 says the sun and moon grow dark; whether that describes a swarm thick enough to block the light, or more, the verse does not say.

title: Hazor, at Tel Hazor
summary: The Hazor of Joshua 11, of Jabin in Deborah's day, of Solomon's building and of Tiglath-pileser's conquest is the mound of Tel Hazor (Tell el-Qedah), north of the Sea of Galilee. OpenBible's survey of 35 reference works finds none that places it elsewhere.
body: Josephus places Hazor 'over the Semechonitis' (Antiquities 5.5.1), the lake whose 'marshes and fens' the Jordan divides before it reaches the Sea of Galilee (Jewish War 3.10.7). M. Luca gives Tel Hazor's place as about 6 km south of the Huleh lake and 15 km north of the Sea of Galilee.

Hazor is named in texts from beyond Israel. Luca lists the Egyptian Execration Texts, letters from Mari, the lists of cities Thutmose III and Amenhotep II claimed at Karnak, and the Amarna letters, in which Hazor's king promises loyalty to the pharaoh (EA 227–228) and the king of Tyre reports him gone over to the ʿapiru (EA 148).

Cuneiform tablets have been found on the mound itself. One, Hazor 5, picked up on its surface, is a court record: in Wayne Horowitz's summary, three attendants bring a suit before the king over 'a home and garden in Hazor', and the king finds for the defendant. Luca writes that a cuneiform fragment found there confirmed the identification.

OpenBible.info's geocoding data records the identifications given in 35 reference works for this Hazor: every one places it at Tel Hazor, 21 of them as certain and 12 as likely, and none proposes another site. When the Late Bronze city was destroyed, and by whom, is a separate question, not taken up here. The Bible's other places named Hazor, in the Negev (Joshua 15:23, 25), in Benjamin (Nehemiah 11:33) and in Arabia (Jeremiah 49:28-33), are different towns.

title: Shiloh, by the road from Bethel to Shechem
summary: Judges 21:19 places Shiloh 'north of Bethel east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah'. S. R. Driver and John Wijngaards find the ruin of Khirbet Seilun where that description puts it. Whether it was also the Shiloh of the tent and the ark is a question of its own.
body: Judges 21:19 gives directions: Shiloh is 'north of Bethel east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.' S. R. Driver (1902), as John Wijngaards quotes him, follows the road north from Beitin (Bethel): Seilun stands 9½ miles north-north-east of it, a little east of the highway, and el-Lubban, 'evidently the Lebonah of Jg 21,19', 3 miles north-north-west of Seilun. Wijngaards credits E. Robinson with finding the site, and Schwartz and Shemesh cite Robinson and Smith for Seilun as the name Shiloh kept.

Eusebius's Onomasticon places Shiloh in Ephraim, where 'the ark remained … until the time of Samuel', 'twelve miles from Neapolis in Akrabattine'; Jerome's Latin makes it ten. Schwartz and Shemesh report four Byzantine churches built at Khirbet Seilun, and that in the Crusader period Shiloh was placed instead at Nabi Samwil.

A Danish team led by Hans Kjaer dug at Khirbet Seilun in the 1920s and 1930s, and Israel Finkelstein in the 1980s. Schwartz and Shemesh write that 'the exact location of the Tabernacle complex at Shiloh has occupied many researchers, and this issue remains in dispute'; Wijngaards notes that neither excavation found a trace of the sanctuary. Whether Khirbet Seilun was the Shiloh of the sanctuary at all is set out in its own card.

title: Where the sanctuary at Shiloh stood
summary: Robinson, Driver, Albright, and Schwartz and Shemesh take Khirbet Seilun for the Shiloh where the tent of meeting and the ark stood. John Wijngaards argues that the sanctuary stood in the valley of Shechem, at Taanath-shiloh, and that Khirbet Seilun is a different Shiloh.
body: For Khirbet Seilun: Judges 21:19's directions fit it, Eusebius places the Shiloh of the ark at about its distance from Neapolis, its name is Shiloh's, and Byzantine Christians built churches there. W. F. Albright, as Wijngaards quotes him, explains why Judges should spell out the way to so famous a place: 'When the Book of Judges was [completed], probably at about 700 BC, the site of Shiloh was evidently abandoned since the redactor deems it necessary to give us the exact description of the place.' Wijngaards reports that most later commentators take the directions as a note of that kind, 'inserted to preserve a record of Shiloh's position'.

Wijngaards (2020), who calls the identification 'almost universally accepted by archaeologists', agrees that Khirbet Seilun is the Shiloh of Judges 21:19, and argues it is not the sanctuary's. In Judges 21 the young women are brought to 'the camp at Shiloh' (21:12), and the elders then direct the Benjamites to a Shiloh they must describe (21:19), which, he writes, the text 'introduces … as an unknown locality'; he finds no sign in the text that the directions are a later note. He reports that the Danish excavations found Seilun uninhabited from about 1050 to 350 BC, while Kings has Ahijah living at Shiloh (1 Kings 14:2-4) and Jeremiah has men coming from Shiloh (41:5), and that no trace of the sanctuary has been found. He proposes Taanath-shiloh, on Ephraim's border (Joshua 16:6), at Khirbet Tana in the valley of Shechem, where his own studies place Israel's early covenant ceremonies.

Wijngaards calls his arguments a 'devil's advocate' and allows that Judges 21:19b 'could, of course, be a gloss skilfully inserted into the text by a later redactor'. He concludes that it 'seems certainly possible, if not likely, that the ancient pre-monarchic sanctuary of Shiloh lay in the valley of Shechem', and that Khirbet Seilun 'might be acceptable as an emergency solution forced on us by defect of anything better.' He also reports an earlier proposal, A. T. Richardson's (1925), of Beit Silo near Beitunia.
